### Applicant 1: Lars Schöbitz

#### 1.1 Work related to research, RDM, RSE, ORD, and the FAIR principles

Lars Schöbitz has been the Open Science Specialist and embedded Data Steward at Global Health Engineering (D-MAVT) since the Chair was founded in July 2021. He supports all group members in RDM, RSE, ORD and the FAIR principles and owns the group's data management strategy. His trainings are hands-on application of RDM workflows that are designed, tested and supported.

He leads openwashdata, a community funded through four ETH ORD projects, where the toolchain is tested under research conditions turning unpublished WASH (Water, Sanitation, Hygiene) datasets into published, documented, citable data packages. He also runs meta-analysis of the sector, covering research and UN global monitoring, to baseline current data sharing practice and monitor how it changes.

For this he designed and taught ds4owd (Data Science for openwashdata), an online course that trained more than 150 participants to manage and publish data using R, Git, and GitHub, with weekly student hours, support on real assignments using participants' own data, and a capstone project. His teaching is grounded in hands-on practice rather than slides: participants finish able to point to how they addressed the FAIR principles in their own data.

It builds on a 4-ECTS class, "Research Beyond the Lab: Open Science and Research Methods for a Global Engineer", designed and taught with Elizabeth Tilley three times (spring 2022, 2024, 2025), in which D-MAVT students ran a research project, collected their own data, learned R, Git, GitHub, and Quarto, and applied FAIR data management, with all material published as Open Educational Resources.

Alongside the openwashdata projects funded by the ETH Domain ORD programme (Measure 1), he supported the funded Explore project FAIRqual with the D-USYS Transdisciplinarity Lab, on how ORD practice differs for qualitative researchers and on the data governance questions behind it.

#### 1.2 Previous and ongoing RDM/RSE activities at ETH Zurich

Lars is a data steward in the ETH Zurich Data Stewardship Network (DSN), hosted by the ETH Library, and holds several roles in the reproducibility and RDM community:

- Data steward, ETH Zurich Data Stewardship Network.
- Local Node Leader for ETH Zurich in the Swiss Reproducibility Network (SwissRN) since 2025.
- Contributor to the AI Disclosure Working Group of the Global Federation of Reproducibility Networks (GFRN), feeding the reproducibility perspective into the Global Reporting Standard for AI Disclosure in Research.
- Member of the Expert Sounding Group for the ETH Domain ORD Measure 5 project "Career Paths for Open Research Data Professionals" (2025 to 2026).

The programme is built on a data-package pipeline Lars has developed and used for years: it produces tidy data, README files, data dictionaries, and archived Zenodo releases through the R ecosystem, with curated websites for discovery. The GHE Open Science Team uses it daily, taking raw data through an audit trail of versioned, documented steps to a published FAIR data package with a DOI, a citation file recording each contributor's ORCID, and an entry in the ETH Research Collection.

He tracks developments in RDM, FAIR, and ORD, including MLCroissant, data-dict.yaml, and RO-Crate (ETH Node), and has presented this workflow under the title "Plan for tomorrow today" at many venues in the reproducibility and RDM communities.

His employment at Global Health Engineering is permanent and runs for the full project duration, so the team can evaluate whether the offer continues beyond twelve months with a yearly cohort from ETH Zurich and FAIR Coalition members.

Earlier gitforsci and agentsforsci workshops, supported by the DSN and SwissRN, produced training material this programme reuses and refines. Because much of the training covers agentic AI programming, that material is kept current and feeds the wider conversation on declaring AI use in research.

### Applicant 2: Adriana Clavijo Daza

#### 1.1 Work related to research, RDM, RSE, ORD, and the FAIR principles

Adriana Clavijo Daza has been a member of the Global Health Engineering Open Science Team since June 2025 and an active contributor of the openwashdata community. She holds an MSc in Statistics and Data Science and is a Carpentries-certified instructor. Before joining ETH, she worked as a statistician and data scientist for public and private institutions in Colombia, as well as for a non-profit and a consultancy firm in Switzerland.

As a Scientific Assistant, Adriana supports the supervision of PhD students by advising on data management and reproducible workflows, develops and maintains R data packages that publish WASH datasets in a documented, reusable form for the openwashdata community and Global Health Engineering. She co-developed and maintains an R package for the openwashdata community that turns a tidy dataset into a documented, installable, citable R package with an accompanying website, substantially lowering the technical barrier to publishing research data in FAIR-compliant form.

As an instructor, she engages with learners, particularly those who need more support in working through the community's offerings. Her teaching training experience focuses on novices and on creating a safe environment in which to fail.

#### 1.2 Previous and ongoing RDM/RSE activities at ETH Zurich

Adriana is a member of the ETH Library Data Stewardship Network, providing a direct link between this project and the DSN that the call asks applicants to support. Her RDM and RSE work at ETH spans training, advising, and software development. She supported the ds4owd course, which trained more than 150 participants, through weekly student hours, direct assistance with assignments, and personalised guidance on the final project. She also hosted data science flipped-classroom sessions with PhD students from Global Health Engineering and Food Systems Economics and Policy, built around the recordings of the ten-week ds4owd course: participants watched the recordings and completed the assignments on their own, then worked hands-on with Adriana in additional training sessions with supplementary exercises.

She also collaborates with PhD students at Global Health Engineering, advising them on the selection of appropriate statistical methods for their data analysis, with a particular focus on reproducibility and transparent research practices with R, Git, GitHub and Quarto. In addition, she contributed a talk on Open Research Data to the D-MAVT course Ethics and Scientific Integrity for Doctoral Students, introducing participants to the principles and practical aspects of sharing research data.

## 2. Project (weight 80%, sub-sections 2.1 to 2.5 weighted equally)

\[TODO three pages maximum for all of section 2. Delete all guiding questions in the DOCX. Keep the five sub-sections balanced in length.\]

### 2.1 Relevance of digital research assets for ETH Zurich

The digital research assets are the participants' own datasets, with the code, workflows, and documentation needed to make them FAIR. Each of the fifteen participants brings real data from their own work: tabular, survey, measurement and sensor data, and the qualitative material (interviews and recordings) that raises the hardest sharing questions.

Agentic AI tools give ETH researchers a second reason to make these assets FAIR. An agent that cleans or reuses a dataset needs the same documentation a human colleague needs, such as a data dictionary stating what each variable means. Researchers who document their data well can hand routine work to an agent and check the result; those who do not, cannot. Agents also produce code and text that reach research outputs, so researchers need a way to declare AI use that shows what they still produced themselves. Participants use these tools on their own data, and the declaration of AI use runs through the whole year (section 2.2).

The gap is practical. ETH researchers know the FAIR principles exist but often cannot apply them to their own data, largely because adopting new workflows costs time that data sharing and computational reproducibility are not yet rewarded for. Over twelve months the programme lets researchers adopt a new workflow alongside existing practice and build the arguments for it, using established teaching methods: spaced practice, hands-on activities, and relevance to the learner's own work.

The target community is ETH researchers who already hold, or are moving into, RDM responsibility, drawn from several departments, career stages, and disciplines. This is the professionalisation angle of the ETH Domain Measure 5 work on career paths for open research data professionals: the programme upskills people who already carry RDM responsibility, increasingly doctoral students, and is a route into the embedded data stewardship role Global Health Engineering already practises. The cohort balances postdoctoral researchers and doctoral students, alongside scientific and technical staff carrying RDM responsibility; one or two professors is an aspirational goal, carrying the practice into how a group is led. Participants are selected for a dataset of their own, some coding experience, and curiosity about agentic AI tools. The mixed cohort is the point: it lets the programme treat FAIR data sharing as something that differs by community and data type, and produce recommendations specific to those communities.

### 2.2 Specific effort that will be funded by this call

The innovation is that participants make their own data FAIR by doing it, with support, across a full year. Most FAIR and RDM training at ETH is delivered as short courses or summer schools that do not touch participants' own data. This programme walks each participant from a raw file to a published, citable data package, then supports them while they apply the same workflow to the rest of their data.

A second innovation runs through the year: the declaration of AI use. As participants apply agentic AI workflows to their own data, the programme treats disclosure as an open question in research integrity and develops practical answers with fifteen real researchers. It asks how researchers show which parts of their work they produced themselves, connecting to Lars's contribution to the GFRN AI Disclosure Working Group. The programme explores provenance trails for AI use, from Git commits that make each AI-assisted change visible and reversible to experimental tools such as re_gent that record which agent step and prompt produced a change.

The applicants' own training is a funded part of the project. Lars Schöbitz and Adriana Clavijo Daza will deepen their skills in agentic AI workflows for data management and in organisational-change methods for embedding open-science practice. The organisational-change workshop, delivered by Greg Wilson (author of "Organisational Change for Open Science"), trains the applicants and the cohort together, and the applicants carry the method into later cohorts and their DSN work.

The five workshops, the data-package pipeline, and the supporting materials become a repeatable offering Global Health Engineering can run for further ETH cohorts after the project:

- Two four-hour workshops on FAIR data sharing and data management, built on the openwashdata workflow, using each participant's own data, with support hours between sessions.
- One four-hour workshop on Git and GitHub or GitLab collaborative workflows.
- One four-hour workshop on GitHub or GitLab for task and project management.
- One eight-hour workshop on agentic AI workflows for data management.
- One full-day organisational-change workshop for open science, delivered by Greg Wilson at Villa Hatt.

Community building runs throughout, as the 2nd call requires. Global Health Engineering will host AI Playground sessions three times per term from spring semester 2027, open to anyone at ETH and to the general public. The playground connects the cohort to the wider research community, their own and beyond ETH. It is a general offering that runs with or without this funding, and taking part is not required of the fifteen. A Matrix (Element) channel, open to every ETH member and to the public, gives live support and links the cohort to that community. Quarterly hands-on team meetings keep participants working between workshops, and 1:1 support from Lars and Adriana is available on request. The cohort itself becomes a cross-department community of practice, as participants read and support each other's data and code.

The expected outputs are published FAIR data packages from fifteen ETH researchers, each able to repeat the workflow on their remaining data, and a tested programme ready for the next community. Because participants come from several departments and career stages, the practice spreads into their groups.

The programme also produces a research output. The fifteen participants are both trainees and a study cohort: over a full year it examines how FAIR data sharing, data security, and the declaration of AI use differ across their disciplines. From this come recommendations on community-specific FAIR practice and on declaring AI use, contributing to the conversation on scientific integrity as AI-assisted workflows reshape research.

The programme runs over twelve months in four work packages, summarised in the table below.

- WP1, Setup and recruitment (months 1 to 2). Complete the cohort to fifteen, continuing the open call with the FAIR Coalition's backing, collect signed commitments, gather each participant's dataset, data description, and RDM competency baseline, set up the ETH GitLab and GitHub spaces and the Matrix channel, and finalise the workshop schedule. Deliverable: a confirmed cohort and a working programme environment. Lead: Lars Schöbitz.
- WP2, Core workshops and data-package delivery (months 2 to 9). Run the five workshops and the support hours between them, with Lars Schöbitz as education lead and Adriana Clavijo Daza supporting every workshop in person and technically. Each participant produces published, FAIR data package from their own data. Deliverables: five workshops delivered, minimum fifteen data packages in progress, support logged through issues. Leads: Lars Schöbitz and Adriana Clavijo Daza, with Greg Wilson for the organisational-change workshop.
- WP3, Community building and outreach (months 1 to 12, running throughout). Day-to-day support through the Matrix channel, 1:1 calls and direct help with each participant's own data, led by Adriana Clavijo Daza; AI playground events and quarterly hands-on team meetings; and outreach through a public project website, blog posts and social media, and talks at RDM and reproducibility venues. Deliverable: an active cross-department community, a public record of the programme, and a record of events. Leads: Adriana Clavijo Daza and Lars Schöbitz.
- WP4, Consolidation, sustainability, and reporting (months 10 to 12). Publish the final data packages, capture the programme as a reusable offering, feed lessons into the DSN, and report. Deliverables: at least fifteen published FAIR data packages, a documented reusable programme, a DSN contribution, a draft data management strategy for each participant's group, final content and financial reports.

Roles: Lars Schöbitz is corresponding applicant and budget manager, leads WP1 and WP4, and is education lead across the workshops. Adriana Clavijo Daza supports every workshop in person and technically, hosts selected modules towards the end, leads the day-to-day support channels and the DSN link, and co-leads WP3. The cohort is divided between the two applicants so each participant has a named contact for their own data. Greg Wilson delivers the organisational-change workshop. Tools are ETH-native and transferable: ETH GitLab, GitHub, Zenodo, the ETH Research Collection, Matrix (Element), R, and Anthropic Claude Code.

### 2.4 Feasibility and risk assessment

The programme builds on proven delivery capability. The Global Health Engineering Open Science Team has already trained more than 150 people to publish open data through ds4owd, and the data-package pipeline and much of the workshop material already exist.

Early-stage proposals were shared with the ETH Library (Julian Dederke) and SwissRN (Daniel Stekhoven, ETHZ local node), so the approach is known to the relevant stakeholders and does not duplicate existing ETH Library courses.

- Recruitment risk: the programme is designed for fifteen participants. At submission seven ETH researchers have expressed interest, recruited through an open call across the Data Stewardship Network, the RSE Network, ETH4D, D-USYS TdLab, and the ETH ORD community. They come from four departments (D-GESS, D-USYS, D-EAPS, D-BAUG) and seven research units: six postdoctoral researchers and one doctoral student, working with measurement and sensor data, surveys, qualitative interview and focus-group material, computational and simulation work, and mixed methods. Mitigation: recruitment continues through WP1, more doctoral students can take senior places if those do not fill, and the FAIR Coalition's reach at ETH can fill remaining places. Interest across four departments within two weeks of an open call suggests demand is not the constraint.
- Drop-out risk: researchers work on unpredictable schedules and availability may change across the year. Mitigation: workshops are recorded so participants can follow the taught elements and exercises later, dates are confirmed early to avoid calendar conflicts, and work between workshops is kept small and manageable, with room for those who want to invest more.
- Financial and eligibility risk: the CHF 30,000 participant-place cost must read as workshop-organisation cost, not staff salary, because personnel costs are not eligible. Mitigation: the budget books it under conferences and workshop organisation, with no salary and no subcontracting line. The concept was shared with openscience\@sl.ethz.ch early and considered appropriate.
- Delivery-capacity risk: two people deliver a year-long programme. Mitigation: the workshop material largely exists, the cohort supports itself, and the AI playground and Matrix channel spread the support load.

Dependencies: ETH GitLab, GitHub, the ETH Research Collection, Zenodo, Villa Hatt availability, and Greg Wilson's availability for the organisational-change workshop. All are either standing ETH infrastructure or confirmable in WP1.

### 2.5 Added value and impact of the project

The project gives ETH a repeatable programme that turns researchers' own data into published FAIR data packages, and leaves it available after the funding ends. The new service is a tested, hands-on FAIR-implementation programme Global Health Engineering can run for further ETH communities, distinct from the principle-level training the DSN and the RDM Summer School provide.

The direct benefit is fifteen published, FAIR, citable data packages from fifteen ETH researchers across several departments, each able to repeat the workflow on the rest of their data and pass it to their group. Because the cohort is mixed by discipline and method, the programme produces a case study of how FAIR data sharing, data security, and the declaration of AI use differ between communities. All teaching material is published as Open Educational Resources, with handbooks on delivering it.

Institutional responsibility sits with the Global Health Engineering Open Science Team, which already runs ORD, RDM, FAIR and AI training as standing activities. Sustainability has two parts. The assets are Open Educational Resources: templates, slides, websites, and an instructor handbook, following the pattern already proven with the Git for Scientists material published through the DSN, and Adriana Clavijo Daza is a certified Carpentries instructor. The competencies travel through the groups participants return to, carried by the data management strategy each participant drafts for their own group. For the FAIR Coalition, the programme is a mechanism to bring more ETH researchers to sign the Charter. The funding model is the per-participant fee: this grant funds and tests the first cohort at CHF 2,000 per place, and later cohorts can fund delivery through the same fee, potentially cross-subsidised through the Coalition.

The project contributes to both communities the call names. Adriana Clavijo Daza is a DSN member, the applicants will sign the FAIR Coalition Charter, and the programme feeds its materials, workflow, and lessons on community-specific FAIR practice back into the DSN, while giving the ETH Library a practical test of the ETH RDM guidelines against real researcher data. The link to the Research Software Engineering community runs through the RSE Network channel, used for recruitment and for sharing results. Lars Schöbitz has proposed a talk to the EnhanceR Symposium 2026 on the approach this programme scales, teaching Git, version control, and coding agents to researchers who do not come from IT, and will deepen that engagement with those responsible for teaching and training at ETH Scientific IT Services.

### 3.2 Justification of expenses

Each requested item is eligible under the call's annex and necessary to deliver the programme.

The training and workshop delivery for the fifteen participants (CHF 30,000) covers organising and running the twelve-month programme: the five workshops, the support hours between them, and the hands-on work that takes each participant's dataset to a published FAIR data package. The cost is CHF 2,000 per participant place, for fifteen places. It is booked as conferences and workshop organisation. It is not a salary or personnel cost; it is the cost of delivering the training service, and the deliverable is fifteen trained researchers and fifteen published data packages.

The organisational-change workshop (CHF 5,000) covers the delivery of a full-day workshop by Greg Wilson on organisational change for open science, held between mid-September and early October 2027. It trains the applicants and the cohort in the methods needed to embed FAIR practice in research groups, which is what turns a set of published data packages into a lasting change of practice. Placing it late in the project means the cohort brings published data packages to the change work. The cost covers honorarium, travel, and three nights of accommodation.

The venue and catering (CHF 5,400) cover running the five workshops. Two of them run a full day and are held at Villa Hatt, the eight-hour agentic AI workflows workshop and the organisational-change workshop, at CHF 1,500 each. The three four-hour workshops are held at ETH at no venue cost. Catering is CHF 30 per person for sixteen people at each of the five workshops.

The software line (CHF 9,000) covers fifteen Claude Code seats for six months, at CHF 100 per seat per month, for the agentic-workflow workshop and the hands-on data-management work following it. The tool is central to the eight-hour agentic-workflow workshop and to the support work between sessions. Its operating cost is covered only to the end of the project, as the annex allows for a project tool. The ETH Library lists AI-powered tools and services for researchers, but the agentic coding tools in that space are listed as unsupported: they are not managed by the ID CCR Cloud Service Center, no cloud assessments are in place, and use is at the researcher's own responsibility. This line therefore does not duplicate a supported ETH service. It gives the cohort a tool on a managed, funded footing for the duration of the programme, and the conditions attached to unsupported tools are themselves part of what the programme teaches: responsible use, what may be sent to a third-party service, and how AI-assisted work is declared are treated as questions the cohort works through on their own data.
